title: Developing Curriculum for Deep Thinking - The Knowledge Revival https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-74661-1 https://tipsforteachers.co.uk/research-developing-curriculum-for-deep-thinking-the-knowledge-revival/
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), January 9, 2025 — original paper:
summary: This page summarizes Surma and colleagues' SpringerBrief arguing for a knowledge-rich curriculum, built on the premise that domain-specific knowledge is what actually enables deep thinking, complex cognitive skills, and equitable access to learning. Drawing on cognitive psychology, educational psychology, and sociology, the authors show how a robust knowledge base underpins reading comprehension and critical thinking rather than existing alongside them as separate skills. They propose a curriculum framework built on content richness, coherence, and clarity, arguing that knowledge should be sequenced systematically across disciplines and grade levels rather than left to accumulate incidentally. Barton's summary highlights that critical thinking is not a generic, transferable skill; it is intertwined with the specific content being thought about, which means teachers must model domain-specific examples of critical thinking rather than teach it in the abstract. The book closes by presenting evidence that knowledge-rich curricula raise achievement and narrow gaps for disadvantaged students, who depend more heavily on school for exposure to advanced vocabulary and content.
points: Critical thinking and other complex cognitive skills are not generic — they are intertwined with domain-specific knowledge, so teachers must model discipline-specific examples of critical thinking rather than teach it as a stand-alone skill.
Disadvantaged students depend disproportionately on school to build advanced vocabulary and rich content knowledge, making a common, content-rich curriculum an equity issue, not just an academic one.
Teachers should sequence topics with attention to the hierarchy and structure within the knowledge itself, since what a learner already knows is the single most important factor shaping new learning.
Making cross-subject connections explicit is a teacher's job, not the student's, since learners struggle to make these connections between fields on their own.
quotes: This SpringerBrief in Education argues for a knowledge-rich curriculum, emphasizing the crucial role of domain-specific knowledge in fostering deep thinking, complex cognitive skills, and equitable educational opportunities.
Teachers must understand that critical thinking and other complex cognitive skills are intertwined with the content of the thoughts themselves, or with domain-specific knowledge.

Teachers should work to build a common knowledge base in the classroom, particularly for disadvantaged students, who depend mostly on schools to be exposed to advanced vocabulary and rich content knowledge.
Teachers need to explicitly make connections regarding concepts between different fields of study, as students have difficulty making these connections themselves.
A knowledge-rich curriculum is the soundest way forward to both effectively teach knowledge and complex skills in school
